question: Your company is adopting Google Cloud. The security team wants one place to apply policies that should affect every project, and the finance, engineering, and marketing departments each want to manage their own projects. What resource hierarchy should you set up?

options.text: Use the organization resource as the root, create a folder per department, and put each department's projects in its folder
options.feedback: The organization node holds company-wide IAM and organization policies, and folders let each department manage its own projects. Policies are inherited from organization to folders to projects.

options.text: Create one project per department and grant each department head the Owner role on the other departments' projects
options.feedback: Projects can't contain other projects, and giving Owner across departments breaks separation. You'd have no central place for company-wide policy.

options.text: Put all projects directly under the organization and use labels to identify each department
options.feedback: Labels help with cost reporting and filtering, but you can't use them as IAM or organization policy boundaries. Folders provide the delegation boundary.

options.text: Create a separate organization for each department
options.feedback: Separate organizations split policy management and make company-wide controls much harder. One organization per company is the recommended pattern.

takeaway: Organization → folders → projects → resources. Policies are inherited downward, so folders are the natural place to delegate administration.

question: You created a project named "Payments Dev" with the project ID payments-dev-4821. A teammate wants to change the project ID to payments-development. What should you tell them?

options.text: Explain that project IDs are permanent, and create a new project if the ID matters
options.feedback: Project IDs are permanent and globally unique. Only the display name can be edited later.

options.text: Change the ID in the console under IAM & Admin > Settings, then save
options.feedback: The Settings page lets you edit the project name, not the project ID.

options.text: Delete the project and immediately create a new project with the same resources
options.feedback: Deleting the project doesn't move resources, and a deleted project's ID can't be reused, so this doesn't help.

options.text: Run gcloud projects update payments-dev-4821 --project-id=payments-development
options.feedback: No such flag exists. Once a project is created, its ID can't be changed.

takeaway: Project name: editable. Project ID: permanent and globally unique. Project number: assigned by Google.

question: Your security team requires that no Compute Engine VM in the organization have an external IP address, except for VMs in one approved project that hosts bastion hosts. What is the most efficient way to enforce this?

options.text: Create a VPC firewall rule in every project that denies all ingress from 0.0.0.0/0 except the bastion
options.feedback: Firewall rules control traffic, not whether a VM gets an external IP. You'd also have to maintain the rule in every project.

options.text: Deny constraints/compute.vmExternalIpAccess at the organization, and allow the bastion VMs in that project
options.feedback: The list constraint blocks external IPs everywhere through inheritance, and a project-level policy can allow specific instances. This is preventive and centrally managed.

options.text: Ask each project owner to remove external IPs, and audit every month with Cloud Asset Inventory reports
options.feedback: Auditing finds violations after the fact. It doesn't prevent them.

options.text: Create a custom IAM role without the compute.instances.create permission and assign it to all developers
options.feedback: Removing create permission stops VM creation entirely rather than just blocking external IPs.

takeaway: Organization policies are preventive guardrails on resource configuration. IAM controls who can act, and org policies control what configurations are allowed.

question: Due to data residency regulations, all resources in your organization's "EU" folder must be created only in European regions. What should you do?

options.text: Require a region=eu label on every resource and alert on resources with non-compliant labels
options.feedback: Labels don't enforce anything, and users can set any label value.

options.text: Create a custom-mode VPC with only European subnets in every project in the EU folder
options.feedback: Subnets limit where VMs can be placed in that network, but they don't stop regional or multi-regional services such as Cloud Storage or BigQuery from being created elsewhere.

options.text: Apply constraints/gcp.resourceLocations on the EU folder with the in:eu-locations value group
options.feedback: The resource locations constraint is inherited by every project in the folder and blocks creation of supported resources outside the allowed locations.

options.text: Grant the EU team a custom role that excludes permissions for non-European regions
options.feedback: IAM permissions aren't scoped by region, so you can't express this with a role.

takeaway: Use constraints/gcp.resourceLocations with value groups such as in:eu-locations for data residency.

question: Your company wants to make sure only identities from its own Cloud Identity domain (example.com) can be granted IAM roles on any resource. A developer was able to grant a role to a personal @gmail.com account. How do you prevent this in the future?

options.text: Configure a VPC Service Controls perimeter around all projects that allows only example.com
options.feedback: VPC Service Controls limit data exfiltration through Google APIs. They don't restrict which principals can appear in IAM policies.

options.text: Remove the resourcemanager.projects.setIamPolicy permission from every developer
options.feedback: Developers would lose the ability to manage any IAM policy, which is too broad. It also doesn't solve the underlying requirement for administrators.

options.text: Enforce constraints/iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains at the organization with only your customer ID
options.feedback: This constraint limits which domains can appear in IAM allow policies. Once enforced, future grants to gmail.com and other outside domains are rejected.

options.text: Enable Data Access audit logs and alert when a gmail.com principal is added
options.feedback: This detects the problem after the fact but doesn't prevent it.

takeaway: Domain restricted sharing (iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains) restricts IAM grants to your own customer IDs.

question: An organization policy at the organization level restricts allowed VM machine types. The data science folder needs to allow additional GPU machine types without affecting other folders. What should you do?

options.text: Set a folder-level policy on data science that merges in the extra GPU machine types
options.feedback: Organization policies can be customized at lower levels. A folder policy can inherit and add allowed values, or replace the parent's policy entirely, for just that subtree.

options.text: Move the data science projects out of the organization so they have no policies
options.feedback: Moving projects out of the organization removes all centralized governance and isn't a recommended practice.

options.text: Open a Google Cloud Support case to exempt the data science folder from the policy
options.feedback: Exemptions are something you configure yourself through the policy hierarchy. Support isn't involved.

options.text: Delete the organization-level policy and recreate the restriction on every other folder
options.feedback: This works, but it's more effort and more error-prone than overriding only where needed.

takeaway: Child resources can inherit, merge with, or override parent organization policies, unless a managed constraint or the policy design prevents it.

question: You just created a new project and run gcloud compute instances list. The command fails with an error saying the Compute Engine API has not been used in the project before or is disabled. What should you do?

options.text: Create a service account and activate it with gcloud auth activate-service-account
options.feedback: Switching identities doesn't help when the API itself is disabled.

options.text: Grant yourself the Compute Admin role on the project
options.feedback: The error is about the API being disabled, not about your permissions.

options.text: Run gcloud services enable compute.googleapis.com in the project
options.feedback: Most Google Cloud APIs must be enabled per project before use. Enabling the Compute Engine API fixes this error.

options.text: Reinstall the Google Cloud CLI with the compute component
options.feedback: gcloud compute commands are part of the core CLI. The error comes from the project's API state, not the local installation.

takeaway: gcloud services enable SERVICE.googleapis.com, and gcloud services list --enabled shows what's on.

question: Your team needs to launch 200 vCPUs of N2 machines in us-central1 for a batch job, but VM creation fails with a QUOTA_EXCEEDED error for N2_CPUS. What should you do?

options.text: Upgrade to Enhanced Support, which raises regional CPU quotas automatically
options.feedback: Quota increases are requested through the quota system. They aren't tied to support plans.

options.text: Request an N2_CPUS quota increase for us-central1 on the Quotas & System Limits page
options.feedback: Quotas are per project and usually per region. You can view current usage and submit an adjustment request from the console or the Cloud Quotas API.

options.text: Change the default region in gcloud to a region with more capacity
options.feedback: That might move the workload, but it doesn't fix the quota in the region you need. Quotas are also per region, and the default region may be just as limited.

options.text: Create the VMs with Spot provisioning, because Spot VMs don't count toward quota
options.feedback: Spot VMs still consume CPU quota (they can draw on preemptible quota where available). Spot doesn't bypass quotas.

takeaway: Quotas protect you and Google Cloud. They're scoped by project and usually by region, and you can request increases.

question: Your company uses Microsoft Active Directory on-premises as the source of truth for employees. You want users and groups to be created and updated automatically in Cloud Identity so you can grant IAM roles to groups. What should you use?

options.text: Create users manually in the Admin console each week from an AD export
options.feedback: This manual process is error-prone and doesn't scale.

options.text: Configure Workforce Identity Federation and then create Cloud Identity accounts for each user
options.feedback: Workforce Identity Federation's point is to avoid syncing identities into Cloud Identity at all. Combining it with manual account creation defeats the purpose.

options.text: Google Cloud Directory Sync (GCDS) to sync users and groups from Active Directory to Cloud Identity
options.feedback: GCDS performs a one-way sync from AD/LDAP to Cloud Identity or Google Workspace, automating user and group lifecycle.

options.text: Ask each employee to sign up for a personal Google Account using their work email
options.feedback: Unmanaged consumer accounts aren't controlled by your organization and won't stay in sync with AD.

takeaway: GCDS syncs AD/LDAP to Cloud Identity automatically. Pair it with SAML SSO so passwords stay in your IdP.

question: Your organization uses Okta as its identity provider. The security team doesn't want to create or synchronize user accounts in Cloud Identity, but employees need to sign in to the Google Cloud console and use gcloud with their Okta identities. What should you configure?

options.text: Workforce Identity Federation with an Okta provider in a workforce pool
options.feedback: Workforce Identity Federation lets users authenticate with an external IdP and get access to Google Cloud without having Cloud Identity accounts.

options.text: A service account per employee, with keys distributed through Okta
options.feedback: Service accounts are for workloads, and distributing keys to people is a serious security risk.

options.text: Workload Identity Federation with an Okta provider
options.feedback: Workload Identity Federation is for workloads (applications and CI systems), not human users signing in to the console.

options.text: Google Cloud Directory Sync, using Okta as the LDAP source
options.feedback: GCDS syncs from LDAP/AD into Cloud Identity, which is exactly what the security team wants to avoid.

takeaway: Workforce Identity Federation is for humans from an external IdP with no sync. Workload Identity Federation is for external workloads.

question: You manage 40 projects. The data analyst team (around 25 people) needs BigQuery Data Viewer on all projects in the "analytics" folder. People join and leave the team often. What is the recommended approach?

options.text: Create a service account for the team and share its key with the analysts
options.feedback: Shared credentials remove accountability and are a security risk.

options.text: Grant the role to each analyst at the organization level so it is inherited
options.feedback: The scope is too broad, since analysts would get access to all projects, and you'd still manage individuals.

options.text: Grant the role to each analyst individually on each of the analytics projects
options.feedback: This means hundreds of bindings to maintain and is easy to get wrong when people change teams.

options.text: Grant the role to an analysts Google group on the analytics folder
options.feedback: Grant roles to groups at the highest level that still respects least privilege. Membership changes then happen in one place, and the folder binding is inherited by every project.

takeaway: Grant roles to groups, not individuals, and bind them at the folder level when many projects need the same access.

question: A security auditor asks for a list of every Cloud Storage bucket in your organization, across hundreds of projects, including ones you didn't know about. What is the fastest way to produce this?

options.text: Query Cloud Logging across all projects for storage.buckets.create entries
options.feedback: Audit logs have limited retention by default and miss buckets created before that window.

options.text: Run gcloud asset search-all-resources at organization scope, filtered to buckets
options.feedback: Cloud Asset Inventory indexes resources across the whole organization and can search or export them in one query.

options.text: Export billing data to BigQuery and list every bucket that has Cloud Storage SKUs
options.feedback: Billing data shows costs, not a reliable inventory, and empty buckets with no charges wouldn't appear.

options.text: Run gcloud storage buckets list in each project with a shell loop
options.feedback: This works but is slow, and it needs project-level permissions everywhere and a complete project list.

takeaway: Cloud Asset Inventory gives an organization-wide view of resources and IAM policies, with search, export, and change feeds.

question: Your compliance team wants to be notified in near real time whenever an IAM policy changes on any project in the "production" folder. What should you set up?

options.text: A Cloud Asset Inventory feed on the folder for IAM policies, publishing to Pub/Sub
options.feedback: Asset feeds send change notifications for resources or IAM policies to Pub/Sub, and they can be scoped to a folder.

options.text: A daily Cloud Scheduler job that exports all IAM policies and compares them
options.feedback: Daily polling isn't near real time and requires custom diff logic.

options.text: Enable Data Access audit logs on all services in the production folder
options.feedback: IAM policy changes are already recorded in Admin Activity logs. Data Access logs don't help, and logs alone don't notify anyone.

options.text: A budget alert on the production folder that emails the compliance team
options.feedback: Budgets track spending, not configuration changes.

takeaway: Asset feeds plus Pub/Sub give near-real-time notification of resource or IAM changes.

question: You're new to a project and want to quickly understand which resources exist and get a natural-language summary of, for example, which VMs are running without recent CPU usage. Which Google Cloud capability is designed for this kind of AI-assisted analysis?

options.text: Cloud Scheduler
options.feedback: Cloud Scheduler is a managed cron service.

options.text: Cloud Deploy
options.feedback: Cloud Deploy is a continuous delivery service for GKE, Cloud Run, and other targets, not an analysis assistant.

options.text: Cloud Shell Editor
options.feedback: Cloud Shell Editor is a browser-based code editor. It doesn't analyze your deployed resources.

options.text: Gemini Cloud Assist
options.feedback: Gemini Cloud Assist is an AI assistant in the console that can analyze your resources, summarize configurations, and help troubleshoot or optimize using natural-language prompts.

takeaway: Gemini Cloud Assist answers questions about your Google Cloud resources, investigates issues, and suggests optimizations.

question: Your company has 12 application projects. The operations team wants a single place to see Cloud Monitoring dashboards and alerts for VMs in all 12 projects. What should you do?

options.text: Export all metrics to BigQuery and build dashboards in Looker Studio
options.feedback: This adds cost and latency and isn't the native way to monitor multiple projects.

options.text: Create a dashboard in each project and bookmark them all
options.feedback: This doesn't give a combined view or allow alerting across projects.

options.text: Create (or choose) a scoping project and add the 12 projects to its metrics scope
options.feedback: A metrics scope lets one scoping project view and alert on metrics from multiple monitored projects.

options.text: Move all 12 projects' VMs into a single project
options.feedback: Consolidating workloads to get monitoring is disruptive and unnecessary.

takeaway: A metrics scope (on a scoping project) aggregates monitoring for multiple projects.

question: Before designing a deployment, you need to confirm that the a3-highgpu-8g machine type is available in europe-west4-a. Which command gives the most direct answer?

options.text: gcloud compute machine-types list --filter="zone:europe-west4-a"
options.feedback: Machine type availability is zonal, and this lists the machine type if it's offered in that zone.

options.text: gcloud compute regions describe europe-west4 --format=json
options.feedback: This shows regional quotas and status, not machine-type availability per zone.

options.text: gcloud compute zones list --filter="name:europe-west4-a"
options.feedback: This confirms the zone exists but says nothing about which machine types it offers.

options.text: gcloud services list --available --filter="name:compute"
options.feedback: This lists APIs, not regional capacity or machine types.

takeaway: Product and machine-type availability varies by region and zone. Check it before you design.

question: A new team member must be able to create projects in the "sandbox" folder but must not be able to modify IAM on other folders. Which role should you grant, and where?

options.text: Project Creator on the sandbox folder
options.feedback: Project Creator grants resourcemanager.projects.create, and binding it on the folder limits project creation to that folder.

options.text: Owner on an existing sandbox project
options.feedback: Owner on a single project doesn't allow creating new projects in the folder.

options.text: Folder Admin on the organization
options.feedback: This lets them manage all folders, including their IAM.

options.text: Organization Administrator on the organization
options.feedback: This is far too much privilege, since it allows managing IAM on the whole organization.

takeaway: Bind roles at the narrowest resource that meets the need. Project Creator on a folder allows creating projects only there.

question: A developer accidentally deleted an important project 10 days ago. What can you do?

options.text: Create a new project with the same project ID and restore resources from snapshots
options.feedback: Project IDs can't be reused, even after deletion.

options.text: Nothing. Project deletion is immediate and permanent
options.feedback: Deletion isn't immediate. Projects enter a pending-deletion (shutdown) state first.

options.text: Run gcloud projects undelete, since deleted projects are recoverable for about 30 days
options.feedback: Deleted projects are shut down and marked for deletion, and an owner can restore them during the roughly 30-day window.

options.text: Open a support case to recover it from Google's backups after 60 days
options.feedback: The recovery window is about 30 days, and you can do it yourself.

takeaway: Deleted projects can be restored for about 30 days with gcloud projects undelete.

question: Every new project in your organization automatically gets a "default" VPC network with permissive firewall rules, which the security team dislikes. How can you stop the default network from being created in new projects?

options.text: Disable the Compute Engine API at the organization level
options.feedback: You can't do that, and you'd lose all VM functionality anyway.

options.text: Enforce constraints/compute.skipDefaultNetworkCreation at the organization
options.feedback: When this boolean constraint is enforced, new projects are created without the default network.

options.text: Create a firewall rule at the organization level that denies all traffic
options.feedback: The default network would still be created, and blocking all traffic would break legitimate workloads.

options.text: Delete the default network in each new project after it's created
options.feedback: This is reactive and easy to forget.

takeaway: Use the skipDefaultNetworkCreation constraint, then create custom-mode VPCs on purpose.

question: You regularly switch between a development project in us-east1 and a production project in europe-west1, each with a different account. What's the most convenient way to manage this in the gcloud CLI?

options.text: Run gcloud init every time you switch and answer the prompts again
options.feedback: gcloud init works, but rerunning the interactive setup each time is slow and unnecessary.

options.text: Add --project and --region flags to every command and log in again each time
options.feedback: This is tedious and error-prone. Configurations handle it for you.

options.text: Create a named gcloud configuration for each environment and activate the one you need
options.feedback: Named configurations store properties such as account, project, and compute/region, and you can switch between them instantly.

options.text: Install two copies of the Google Cloud CLI in separate folders, one per account
options.feedback: That's unnecessary, since configurations exist for exactly this case.

takeaway: gcloud config configurations let you switch account, project, and region in one step.

question: Your organization was just created when you verified your Cloud Identity domain. No one can create folders yet. Who should grant folder-management permissions, and what's a good first step?

options.text: The billing account administrator, by linking a billing account
options.feedback: Billing roles don't grant resource hierarchy permissions.

options.text: Any project owner, by granting Folder Admin on their project
options.feedback: Folder Admin isn't meaningful at the project level, and project owners can't manage organization-level IAM.

options.text: Google Cloud Support, by opening a ticket to bootstrap folder permissions
options.feedback: Google Support doesn't grant IAM roles in your organization.

options.text: A Cloud Identity Super Admin, who grants Organization Administrator to cloud admins
options.feedback: When an organization is created, Super Admins can assign the Organization Administrator role, and Organization Administrators then manage IAM for the hierarchy.

takeaway: The Cloud Identity Super Admin bootstraps the organization by granting Organization Administrator to cloud admins (preferably groups).

question: A contractor needs to view all resources in a project but must not be able to change anything or see data inside Cloud Storage objects or BigQuery tables. Which choice best follows least privilege?

options.text: Narrow predefined viewer roles or a custom role with only metadata permissions
options.feedback: The basic Viewer role includes read access to data in many services. Combining narrower predefined roles, or building a custom role, limits access to metadata.

options.text: Editor, limited by an IAM condition to read-only methods
options.feedback: Editor allows modifying most resources.

options.text: Owner, with the contractor asked not to make changes
options.feedback: Owner grants full control, including IAM changes.

options.text: Security Reviewer only, granted on the contractor's project
options.feedback: Security Reviewer allows listing IAM policies but doesn't grant viewing of all resources.

takeaway: Basic roles are broad. Viewer can read data in many services, so prefer predefined or custom roles.

question: The finance team wants to break down Google Cloud costs by team and environment across many projects. What's the simplest way to make this possible?

options.text: Create a separate billing account for each team
options.feedback: Multiple billing accounts make invoicing and discounts harder. Labels are simpler.

options.text: Add team and env network tags to every VM and filter billing reports by tag
options.feedback: Network tags are used by firewall rules and routes. They don't appear in billing data.

options.text: Apply team and env labels to resources and group costs by label in billing reports
options.feedback: Labels are key-value pairs that flow into billing data and can be used for filtering and grouping costs.

options.text: Name every resource with a team prefix and parse names in a spreadsheet
options.feedback: This relies on naming discipline and manual work, while labels give native cost breakdown.

takeaway: Labels are for cost allocation and filtering. Network tags are for firewall and route targeting.

question: Your security team wants to conditionally allow a group to administer only VMs in projects tagged as environment=dev, and to use the same tag with organization policies. Which feature supports this?

options.text: Network tags on the VMs
options.feedback: Network tags apply only to VM firewall and route targeting.

options.text: Resource Manager tags (secure tags)
options.feedback: Tags are created at the organization or project level, attached to resources, and inherited. IAM conditions and organization policies can use them to grant or enforce conditionally.

options.text: Labels on the projects and VMs
options.feedback: Labels are metadata for organization and billing. You can't use them in IAM conditions or organization policy conditions.

options.text: Folder display names in conditions
options.feedback: You can't use folder display names as conditions.

takeaway: Resource Manager tags (secure tags) support IAM conditions, org policy conditions, and Cloud NGFW targeting. Labels don't.

question: You want to be alerted before your project runs out of a regional quota (for example, in-use IP addresses), so you can request an increase in time. What should you do?

options.text: Enable Data Access audit logs for Compute Engine and alert on address creation
options.feedback: Audit logs record API calls but don't show quota consumption trends.

options.text: Check the Quotas & System Limits page every week and export the results
options.feedback: Manual checks can miss sudden growth, while alerts are proactive.

options.text: Create a billing budget for the project with an alert threshold at 80%
options.feedback: Budgets track spend, not resource quotas.

options.text: Create a Cloud Monitoring alerting policy on quota usage as a ratio of the limit, at 80%
options.feedback: Quota usage and limits are exported as Cloud Monitoring metrics, so you can alert before you hit the limit.

takeaway: Alert on quota metrics in Cloud Monitoring to stay ahead of quota limits.

question: You plan to enforce a new organization policy that blocks service account key creation across the organization. You're worried it will break existing automation. What's the safest way to roll this out?

options.text: Remove the iam.serviceAccountKeys.create permission from all roles with a script
options.feedback: You can't change predefined roles, and this is the wrong tool.

options.text: Apply it only to a single test project forever
options.feedback: A single project doesn't give organization-wide protection.

options.text: Create the policy in dry-run mode, fix the workloads it flags, then enforce it
options.feedback: Dry-run organization policies log violations without blocking, which lets you assess impact before enforcing.

options.text: Enforce it at the organization level immediately and fix whatever breaks
options.feedback: Enforcing without assessment risks outages.

takeaway: Use dry-run organization policies or Policy Simulator to safely assess a constraint before enforcing it.

question: Which statement best describes the relationship between projects and resources in Google Cloud?

options.text: Each resource belongs to one project, where APIs and billing are managed
options.feedback: Projects organize resources and are where APIs are enabled and billing is attached.

options.text: Projects are optional. Resources can exist directly under folders
options.feedback: Most resources must live inside a project. Folders contain projects, not resources.

options.text: A resource can belong to several projects at the same time
options.feedback: Each resource belongs to exactly one project, though Shared VPC lets other projects use a host project's network.

options.text: A project can be linked to multiple billing accounts at once
options.feedback: A project is linked to at most one billing account at a time.

takeaway: Projects are the base unit for APIs, billing, quotas, and most IAM.

question: Your company syncs AD users to Cloud Identity with GCDS. Users complain about having two passwords. What should you configure?

options.text: Disable 2-step verification for all synced users so sign-in is faster
options.feedback: This weakens security and doesn't remove the second password.

options.text: Workload Identity Federation with Active Directory as the provider
options.feedback: That's for workloads, not user sign-in.

options.text: SAML single sign-on in Cloud Identity, with your corporate IdP as the provider
options.feedback: With SSO, Cloud Identity redirects authentication to your IdP, so users have one corporate password.

options.text: Sync password hashes with GCDS and have users reset passwords monthly
options.feedback: Users would still manage credentials in Google, and the complaint remains.

takeaway: GCDS handles provisioning and SAML SSO handles authentication. Together they give users one identity.

question: You want to see all APIs that are currently enabled in your project and then disable the unused Cloud Translation API. Which commands should you use?

options.text: gcloud components list, then gcloud components remove translate
options.feedback: Components are local CLI parts, not project APIs.

options.text: gcloud services list --enabled, then gcloud services disable translate.googleapis.com
options.feedback: These commands list enabled services and disable a specific one in the active project.

options.text: gcloud apis list, then gcloud apis remove translate
options.feedback: These aren't valid gcloud command groups.

options.text: gcloud projects describe, then gcloud projects update --disable-api=translate
options.feedback: Project describe doesn't show enabled APIs, and there's no such update flag.

takeaway: gcloud services list --enabled, gcloud services enable, and gcloud services disable manage project APIs.

question: Your organization wants to prevent anyone from creating GKE clusters that don't have Workload Identity Federation for GKE enabled. No predefined organization policy constraint covers this exact setting. What should you do?

options.text: Set a budget alert on GKE that fires when a noncompliant cluster is created
options.feedback: Budgets don't enforce configuration.

options.text: Use Cloud Asset Inventory to detect noncompliant clusters and delete them daily
options.feedback: This is reactive cleanup, not prevention.

options.text: Grant developers a custom IAM role that excludes container.clusters.create
options.feedback: This blocks all cluster creation, not just noncompliant clusters.

options.text: Create and enforce a custom organization policy constraint on the cluster's workload identity field
options.feedback: Custom constraints let you write conditions on supported resource fields (including many GKE fields) to allow or deny create and update operations.

takeaway: Custom organization policy constraints (CEL on resource fields) cover settings that predefined constraints don't.

question: A colleague needs to run gcloud and kubectl commands from a locked-down laptop where they can't install software. What's the quickest option?

options.text: Set up Cloud Workstations with a custom image that includes the CLI tools
options.feedback: This is powerful but heavier than needed for quick CLI access.

options.text: Use Cloud Shell in the console, where gcloud and kubectl are preinstalled
options.feedback: Cloud Shell is a free browser-based shell with a persistent 5 GB home directory and preinstalled tools.

options.text: Install the Cloud SDK in a Docker container on the laptop
options.feedback: They can't install software, so Docker is ruled out too.

options.text: Use a Compute Engine VM with an external IP and install tools there
options.feedback: This works but takes setup, costs money, and exposes a VM.

takeaway: Cloud Shell gives a ready-to-use, authenticated CLI environment in the browser.

question: A user has the Compute Admin role granted on folder "engineering" and the Compute Viewer role on project "eng-web", which is in that folder. What effective access does the user have on eng-web?

options.text: No compute access, because the conflicting roles cancel out
options.feedback: Roles never cancel each other out. Only deny policies can remove permissions.

options.text: Compute Viewer only, because the project-level binding overrides the folder
options.feedback: IAM allow policies are additive. A lower-level grant doesn't remove inherited permissions.

options.text: Compute Admin only on resources created after the folder binding
options.feedback: Inheritance applies to all resources regardless of when they were created.

options.text: Compute Admin, because inherited and project grants are combined
options.feedback: Permissions granted higher in the hierarchy are inherited, so the user gets the union of both roles.

takeaway: Allow policies are additive and inherited. Only IAM deny policies can subtract permissions.

question: A group has Editor inherited from the organization. You need to make sure nobody in that group can delete Cloud SQL instances in the "finance-prod" project, without changing the organization-level grant. What should you use?

options.text: An IAM deny policy on the finance-prod project that denies cloudsql.instances.delete for the group
options.feedback: Deny policies are evaluated before allow policies and override any granted permissions for the specified principals.

options.text: An organization policy that disables Cloud SQL
options.feedback: That blocks the whole service, which isn't the requirement.

options.text: A project-level allow policy granting Cloud SQL Viewer to the group
options.feedback: Allow policies are additive. Viewer doesn't remove the inherited Editor permissions.

options.text: Remove the group from the organization and add it back to each project except finance-prod
options.feedback: That changes the organization-level grant, which the requirement says not to do, and it means a lot of rework.

takeaway: IAM deny policies block specific permissions for principals regardless of allow grants.

question: You're setting up networking for a new environment. You need full control over subnet IP ranges so they don't overlap with on-premises networks you'll connect to later. Which VPC mode should you choose?

options.text: Default network
options.feedback: The default network is an auto mode VPC with permissive default firewall rules.

options.text: Legacy network
options.feedback: Legacy networks are deprecated and have no subnets.

options.text: Custom mode VPC
options.feedback: Custom mode lets you choose which regions get subnets and exactly which IP ranges they use.

options.text: Auto mode VPC
options.feedback: Auto mode creates one subnet per region from a fixed 10.128.0.0/9 range, which may overlap with on-premises ranges.

takeaway: Use custom mode VPCs in production so you control the IP plan. You can convert auto mode to custom, but not back.

question: Your organization wants security bulletins and technical notifications from Google Cloud to reach the security team's mailing list instead of individual project owners. What should you configure?

options.text: A Cloud Monitoring notification channel set to the security mailing list
options.feedback: Monitoring channels deliver your alerts, not Google's account notifications.

options.text: A Pub/Sub topic subscribed to Google's release notes
options.feedback: That isn't how account notifications are delivered.

options.text: Essential Contacts at the organization for the Security and Technical categories
options.feedback: Essential Contacts route Google Cloud notifications by category to the right people or groups, and they're inherited down the hierarchy.

options.text: Grant the security team the Owner role on all projects
options.feedback: This is overprivileged and doesn't route notifications reliably.

takeaway: Essential Contacts route Google Cloud notifications (billing, security, technical, legal) to the right teams.

question: Your operations team wants to know automatically when a Google Cloud incident affects the products and regions their projects use, and to see this in one console page. What should they use?

options.text: The public Google Cloud Status Dashboard only
options.feedback: The public dashboard isn't personalized to your projects and can't send notifications for your specific resources.

options.text: Personalized Service Health with incident alerts
options.feedback: Personalized Service Health shows incidents that affect your projects and integrates with alerts and notifications.

options.text: Recommender insights for each project
options.feedback: Recommender gives optimization suggestions, not incident notifications.

options.text: Cloud Trace with latency alerts
options.feedback: Cloud Trace analyzes application latency, not Google platform incidents.

takeaway: Personalized Service Health is project-relevant incident visibility and alerting.

question: You created a new project, but you can't create any Compute Engine VMs. The console says billing must be enabled. What should you do?

options.text: Grant yourself the Compute Admin role
options.feedback: The issue is billing, not permissions.

options.text: Enable the Cloud Billing API only
options.feedback: Enabling the API doesn't link a billing account.

options.text: Request a Compute Engine quota increase
options.feedback: Without billing, you can't use the service at all, so quota isn't the issue.

options.text: Link the project to a billing account
options.feedback: Many services, including Compute Engine, require the project to be linked to a billing account.

takeaway: Billable services require the project to be linked to an active billing account.

question: A developer has the Owner role on a project and wants to link it to the company's billing account, but the operation fails. What additional permission do they most likely need?

options.text: Billing Account Viewer on the billing account
options.feedback: Viewer can't link projects.

options.text: Billing Account User on the billing account
options.feedback: Linking requires permissions on both sides: on the project (Owner or Project Billing Manager) and on the billing account (Billing Account User or Administrator).

options.text: Project Billing Manager on the organization
options.feedback: Project Billing Manager covers the project side, which Owner already has. The missing permission is on the billing account.

options.text: Organization Administrator on the organization
options.feedback: This doesn't include billing account permissions.

takeaway: Linking a project needs permission on the project and on the billing account (Billing Account User).

question: Your manager asks that the team get an email when this month's spending on the "ml-research" project reaches 50%, 90%, and 100% of $2,000, and also when forecasted spend is expected to exceed $2,000. What should you do?

options.text: Set a $2,000 quota cap on the project's billable services
options.feedback: Quotas limit resource usage, not dollars, and don't send budget emails.

options.text: Export billing to BigQuery and check it manually each week
options.feedback: This isn't automated or timely.

options.text: Create a Cloud Monitoring alert when the project's total CPU utilization passes 90%
options.feedback: CPU utilization isn't spend.

options.text: A $2,000 project budget with actual thresholds at 50/90/100% and a forecasted one at 100%
options.feedback: Budgets support both actual and forecasted thresholds and email billing admins or other configured recipients.

takeaway: Budgets alert on actual or forecasted spend, and they don't stop spending by themselves.

question: A research project must never exceed $500 per month. Exceeding it, even briefly, is unacceptable, and the team accepts that services will stop. What's the recommended way to implement this?

options.text: Set a project quota of 500 "dollars per month" for all services
options.feedback: No such quota exists. Quotas limit resource counts and rates, not money.

options.text: Send budget notifications to Pub/Sub and have a function disable billing at the threshold
options.feedback: Programmatic budget notifications can trigger automation, such as disabling billing, to cap costs. Note that cost data has some delay.

options.text: Create a budget with a 100% threshold. Google Cloud automatically stops services when the budget is reached
options.feedback: Budgets only notify. They don't cap or stop spending.

options.text: Buy committed use discounts sized to $500 per month
options.feedback: Commitments reduce prices but don't cap spending.

takeaway: Budgets notify, and they automate only through Pub/Sub plus a function you write. Disabling billing stops paid services.

question: The finance team wants to analyze detailed, resource-level Google Cloud costs with SQL and build dashboards. What should you set up?

options.text: Detailed Cloud Billing export to BigQuery, queried with SQL
options.feedback: The detailed export includes resource-level cost data in BigQuery for SQL analysis and dashboards.

options.text: Download the PDF invoice each month and import it into a spreadsheet
options.feedback: Invoices aren't granular and the process is manual.

options.text: Cloud Logging sink of billing logs to Cloud Storage
options.feedback: Billing data isn't exported through log sinks.

options.text: Cloud Asset Inventory export to BigQuery, joined with prices
options.feedback: Asset inventory has resource metadata, not costs.

takeaway: Enable billing export to BigQuery early. Exports start from when they're enabled.

question: An accountant must be able to see costs and invoices for the billing account but must not be able to change payment methods or link projects. Which role is appropriate?

options.text: Billing Account Administrator
options.feedback: Administrators can manage payment methods and link projects.

options.text: Billing Account Viewer
options.feedback: Viewer can see cost information and transactions without modifying the billing account.

options.text: Billing Account User
options.feedback: Billing Account User allows linking projects to the account.

options.text: Project Billing Manager
options.feedback: This role manages project-billing linkage, not cost viewing on the account.

takeaway: Billing Account Administrator manages everything, Billing Account User links projects, and Billing Account Viewer only reads.

question: Your company wants to move a project from an old team's billing account to the central finance billing account without downtime. What should you do?

options.text: Link the project to the central billing account with gcloud billing projects link
options.feedback: Changing a project's billing account doesn't interrupt running resources, as long as the new account is active.

options.text: Create a billing subaccount and migrate resources one by one
options.feedback: Subaccounts are for resellers, and moving resources between projects isn't required.

options.text: Delete and recreate the project under the new billing account
options.feedback: This is disruptive, and the project ID can't be reused.

options.text: Open a support case to transfer the project between billing accounts
options.feedback: You can do this yourself with the right billing permissions.

takeaway: gcloud billing projects link PROJECT_ID --billing-account=ACCOUNT_ID changes the billing account without downtime.

question: You want a quick visual of which services drove last month's cost increase, without setting up any exports. Where should you look?

options.text: Cloud Billing Reports, grouped by service
options.feedback: Billing Reports provide built-in cost visualization with grouping and filtering.

options.text: Cloud Asset Inventory change history
options.feedback: Asset Inventory shows resources, not spend.

options.text: Cloud Monitoring dashboards
options.feedback: These show performance metrics, not costs.

options.text: Cloud Logging Logs Explorer
options.feedback: Logs don't show costs.

takeaway: Billing Reports are for quick visual analysis. BigQuery export is for deep or custom analysis.

question: You created a budget for a billing account, but the engineering leads (who aren't billing administrators) say they never receive budget emails. What should you do?

options.text: Create a log-based metric on budget events and alert the leads on it
options.feedback: Budgets don't generate logs you can alert on that way.

options.text: Grant them Billing Account Administrator
options.feedback: This is excessive privilege just to receive alerts.

options.text: Add them as Owners of the projects the budget covers
options.feedback: Owners don't automatically receive billing-account budget emails, and Owner is overprivileged.

options.text: Connect Cloud Monitoring notification channels to the budget
options.feedback: By default, budget emails go to billing admins and users. You can add Monitoring notification channels to reach other recipients.

takeaway: Budget alerts can notify extra recipients through Cloud Monitoring notification channels.

question: A startup is ready for production and wants to be billed monthly by invoice instead of by credit card. What type of Cloud Billing account do they need?

options.text: A billing subaccount under a reseller
options.feedback: Subaccounts are for resellers.

options.text: Self-serve (online) billing account
options.feedback: Self-serve accounts are charged automatically to a card or bank account.

options.text: A free-trial account upgraded to paid
options.feedback: Free-trial accounts can't be invoiced.

options.text: An invoiced (offline) billing account
options.feedback: Invoiced billing is for eligible businesses, with monthly invoices paid by check or wire transfer.

takeaway: Self-serve billing is charged to a card or bank account. Invoiced billing is paid by invoice and requires approval.

question: After enabling the BigQuery billing export, finance notices that costs for some VMs don't show the team label they expected. The labels were added to the VMs yesterday. What's the most likely explanation?

options.text: Labels apply only to usage recorded after they're added
options.feedback: Billing data reflects the labels present when the usage occurred, and isn't rewritten retroactively.

options.text: Billing export only shows project labels
options.feedback: Resource labels are included for supported resources.

options.text: They must enable Data Access audit logs for Compute Engine first
options.feedback: Audit logs aren't related to cost labels.

options.text: Labels on VMs never appear in billing exports
options.feedback: Resource labels do appear in billing data for supported resources.

takeaway: Labels in billing data apply only from when the label is added, so label resources early.

question: Before migrating, you want to estimate the monthly cost of 10 n2-standard-4 VMs, 2 TB of Standard Cloud Storage, and a Cloud SQL instance. What should you use?

options.text: Recommender cost insights
options.feedback: Recommender analyzes existing resources for savings.

options.text: Cloud Billing Reports
options.feedback: Billing Reports show historical spend, not hypothetical estimates.

options.text: The Pricing Calculator
options.feedback: The Pricing Calculator estimates costs for planned configurations before you deploy.

options.text: Cloud Asset Inventory
options.feedback: Asset Inventory lists existing resources.

takeaway: Pricing Calculator is for planning, Billing Reports show actuals, and Recommender helps optimize.

question: You want to allow a group of platform engineers to create and manage folders under the organization, but not grant IAM permissions on projects. Which role should you grant at the organization level?

options.text: Folder Creator or Folder Editor
options.feedback: Folder roles control folder creation and management without broad project IAM permissions.

options.text: Project IAM Admin on the organization
options.feedback: This manages project IAM, which is the opposite of the requirement.

options.text: Owner on every project
options.feedback: This grants far more than needed.

options.text: Organization Administrator
options.feedback: This includes setting IAM on the organization and its resources, which is more than required.

takeaway: Use the specific Resource Manager roles (Folder Creator, Folder Editor, Project Creator) instead of Organization Administrator when possible.

question: You're preparing a new Google Cloud organization for enterprise use. Which two actions are recommended early on? (Choose two.)

options.text: Keep every workload in a single project to simplify billing
options.feedback: A single project removes isolation and IAM boundaries. Labels and billing export handle cost analysis.

options.text: Grant administrative roles to groups instead of individual users
options.feedback: Groups simplify access management and auditing as staff change.

options.text: Grant the Owner role to all developers at the organization level so they aren't blocked
options.feedback: Broad Owner grants violate least privilege and are a major risk.

options.text: Use the default network in production projects to save time
options.feedback: The default network has broad firewall rules and an auto-mode IP plan, so it's not suited to production.

options.text: Set baseline organization policies, such as disabling service account key creation and restricting resource locations
options.feedback: Organization policies create preventive guardrails across the hierarchy from day one.

takeaway: Early guardrails: groups for IAM, baseline org policies, custom VPCs, and a folder structure.

question: You need to deploy a stateless containerized REST API that has unpredictable traffic, sometimes zero requests for hours. The team doesn't want to manage servers or clusters and wants to pay as little as possible when idle. Which service should you choose?

options.text: Compute Engine managed instance group with autoscaling
options.feedback: MIGs can autoscale, but they keep at least one VM running and you manage the OS.

options.text: Compute Engine Spot VM
options.feedback: Spot VMs are cheap but can be preempted, need management, and don't scale to zero by themselves.

options.text: Cloud Run
options.feedback: Cloud Run runs containers serverlessly, scales on requests, and can scale to zero, so you pay nothing for idle time with default settings.

options.text: GKE Standard cluster
options.feedback: You manage node pools and pay for nodes even when idle.

takeaway: Stateless HTTP containers with spiky or zero traffic and no ops point to Cloud Run.

question: You need a small piece of code to run every time a new image is uploaded to a Cloud Storage bucket. It should generate a thumbnail. You don't want to build or manage a container. What's the simplest option?

options.text: A GKE CronJob that polls the bucket every minute
options.feedback: Polling adds latency and you have to operate a cluster.

options.text: A Cloud Run function with a Cloud Storage (object finalized) trigger
options.feedback: Cloud Run functions run source code in response to events, and Google builds the container for you.

options.text: A BigQuery scheduled query
options.feedback: BigQuery can't process image files.

options.text: A Compute Engine VM running a script with gsutil in a loop
options.feedback: This is always-on infrastructure, it polls, and it needs patching.

takeaway: Event-driven, single-purpose code with no container to manage fits Cloud Run functions with an event trigger.

question: A vendor application requires a specific Linux kernel module, must run on a custom OS image, and is licensed per physical core. Which compute option fits best?

options.text: GKE Autopilot with a custom node image
options.feedback: Autopilot manages nodes and restricts node-level customization.

options.text: Cloud Run functions with a custom runtime
options.feedback: Functions run your code in a managed runtime without OS control.

options.text: Cloud Run with a privileged container
options.feedback: Cloud Run abstracts the OS and kernel, so you can't load custom kernel modules.

options.text: Compute Engine on sole-tenant nodes
options.feedback: Compute Engine gives full control of the OS and kernel. Sole-tenant nodes provide dedicated physical servers for bring-your-own-license scenarios.

takeaway: Kernel or OS control points to Compute Engine, and per-core licensing points to sole-tenant nodes.

question: Your team built an AI agent with the Agent Development Kit (ADK). They want a managed, scalable environment that handles sessions and long-term memory for the agent, without running their own Kubernetes cluster. Where should they deploy it?

options.text: Compute Engine VM with a startup script
options.feedback: This works, but you'd manage scaling, sessions, and memory yourself.

options.text: Cloud Storage static website hosting
options.feedback: Static hosting can't run agent code.

options.text: Dataflow running the agent as a streaming job
options.feedback: Dataflow runs data pipelines, not interactive agents.

options.text: Agent Runtime on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform
options.feedback: Agent Runtime is a managed runtime for deploying and scaling agents, with managed sessions and Memory Bank for persistent context.

takeaway: Managed hosting for ADK or other agents, with sessions and memory, means Agent Runtime on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform.

question: You're creating a Compute Engine VM with an attached NVIDIA GPU. During host maintenance events, what availability policy must you set for the VM?

options.text: On host maintenance: Migrate (live migration)
options.feedback: Live migration isn't supported for most GPU VMs, which is why the setting is required.

options.text: Provisioning model: Spot, so maintenance is skipped
options.feedback: Spot affects preemption and pricing, not maintenance behavior.

options.text: On host maintenance: Terminate, typically with automatic restart enabled
options.feedback: VMs with most attached GPUs can't be live migrated, so they must stop during maintenance. Automatic restart brings them back afterward.

options.text: No setting is needed, since GPUs are hot-swapped transparently
options.feedback: GPUs aren't hot-swapped during maintenance.

takeaway: GPU VMs use onHostMaintenance=TERMINATE, and automaticRestart=true brings them back.

question: Your security team wants SSH access to Linux VMs managed through IAM instead of distributing SSH keys in project metadata, and wants access removed automatically when an employee leaves. What should you configure?

options.text: Add each employee's public key to project-wide metadata
options.feedback: Keys in metadata aren't tied to IAM, and they're easy to forget to remove.

options.text: Route SSH through Cloud NAT so connections come from one audited IP
options.feedback: Cloud NAT provides outbound internet access for private VMs. It doesn't manage SSH access.

options.text: Enable OS Login and grant the OS Login IAM roles to the users who need SSH
options.feedback: OS Login links Linux accounts to Google identities and uses IAM. Removing a user from Cloud Identity revokes access.

options.text: Create a bastion host with a shared admin key that's rotated quarterly
options.feedback: Shared keys remove accountability.

takeaway: OS Login ties SSH access to IAM roles (osLogin or osAdminLogin) and supports 2-step verification.

question: A specific VM must not accept SSH keys that are stored in project-wide metadata, while other VMs in the project should still accept them. What should you do?

options.text: Delete all project-wide SSH keys
options.feedback: This affects every VM in the project.

options.text: Change the VM's service account to one without SSH roles
options.feedback: Service accounts don't control which SSH keys a VM accepts.

options.text: Set block-project-ssh-keys=TRUE on that VM
options.feedback: This instance-level setting ignores project-wide SSH keys for that VM only.

options.text: Remove the VM's external IP address
options.feedback: SSH could still be possible through IAP or a bastion, and the keys would still be accepted.

takeaway: block-project-ssh-keys=TRUE on an instance ignores project-level metadata keys.

question: A database VM needs 80,000 IOPS, but only 500 GB of capacity. With Persistent Disk, performance scales with size, so you'd have to overprovision capacity. Which option lets you provision IOPS independently of capacity?

options.text: Hyperdisk with provisioned IOPS
options.feedback: Hyperdisk lets you provision capacity, IOPS, and throughput separately, which avoids overprovisioning capacity for performance.

options.text: pd-balanced at 500 GB
options.feedback: Balanced PD performance also scales with size and has a lower ceiling.

options.text: pd-standard at 500 GB
options.feedback: Standard PD is HDD-backed, has low IOPS, and performance still scales with size.

options.text: Cloud Storage FUSE mounts
options.feedback: Object storage mounted with FUSE isn't suitable for low-latency database block I/O.

takeaway: Hyperdisk provisions performance independently of capacity. Persistent Disk performance scales with size.

question: A rendering job needs a very fast scratch disk for temporary files. The data can be regenerated if lost. What's the most cost-effective high-performance choice?

options.text: pd-standard
options.feedback: It's cheap, but too slow for heavy scratch I/O.

options.text: Filestore Enterprise
options.feedback: A managed NFS share adds network latency and cost you don't need for local scratch.

options.text: Regional Persistent Disk
options.feedback: Regional PD adds synchronous replication across zones, which you don't need for scratch data.

options.text: Local SSD
options.feedback: Local SSDs are physically attached and offer very high IOPS and low latency. Data doesn't persist when the VM stops, which is fine for scratch.

takeaway: Local SSD is ephemeral and very fast, which suits scratch and cache. Use persistent disks for anything that must survive.

question: A single-VM stateful application must survive a zonal outage with minimal data loss (RPO near zero), and you can accept a manual failover to a VM in another zone. Which storage option supports this?

options.text: Cloud Storage Nearline mounted with Cloud Storage FUSE
options.feedback: Object storage isn't a block device for a running application.

options.text: Local SSD in each zone, synchronized with rsync every minute
options.feedback: Local SSDs aren't replicated and don't survive VM loss.

options.text: Regional Persistent Disk, force-attached to a standby VM in the other zone
options.feedback: Regional disks write synchronously to two zones, so you can attach the disk to a VM in the surviving zone after a failure.

options.text: A daily snapshot schedule, restoring to a new VM in another zone
options.feedback: Snapshots give an RPO of up to a day, not near zero.

takeaway: Regional PD or Hyperdisk HA gives synchronous cross-zone replication, near-zero RPO, and failover by force-attach.

question: You need a web tier of identical VMs that automatically replaces unhealthy instances and scales between 2 and 20 instances based on CPU. What should you create?

options.text: Ten individual VMs behind a load balancer
options.feedback: There's no autoscaling or autohealing.

options.text: A managed instance group from a template, with autoscaling and autohealing
options.feedback: MIGs create identical VMs from a template, autoscale on signals like CPU, and recreate instances that fail health checks.

options.text: A Cloud Scheduler job that runs gcloud to resize hourly
options.feedback: This is crude and doesn't react to real-time load.

options.text: An unmanaged instance group with a load balancer health check
options.feedback: Unmanaged groups don't autoscale or autoheal.

takeaway: Instance template plus MIG plus autoscaler plus autohealing health check is the standard elastic VM pattern.

question: Your MIG-based application must remain available if an entire zone fails. What should you do?

options.text: Use a zonal MIG with a larger maximum size
options.feedback: All instances would still be in one zone.

options.text: Use a regional MIG that spreads instances across zones
options.feedback: Regional MIGs spread instances across zones and maintain capacity if one zone becomes unavailable.

options.text: Use a Spot VM template so capacity is pulled from any zone
options.feedback: Spot affects pricing and preemption, not zonal redundancy.

options.text: Take hourly snapshots of every instance
options.feedback: Snapshots help recovery but don't provide availability.

takeaway: Regional MIGs spread instances across zones for high availability.

question: A fault-tolerant batch job processes images in parallel and can be restarted if interrupted. You want to minimize compute cost. What should you use?

options.text: Sole-tenant nodes
options.feedback: These are dedicated hosts and cost more.

options.text: Committed use discounts for 3 years
options.feedback: Commitments suit steady, long-running workloads, not occasional batch jobs.

options.text: Large standard on-demand VMs
options.feedback: This is the most expensive option for interruptible work.

options.text: Spot VMs
options.feedback: Spot VMs offer deep discounts and can be preempted at any time. That's ideal for fault-tolerant, interruptible batch work.

takeaway: Fault-tolerant, interruptible work belongs on Spot VMs, which have no maximum runtime and can be preempted at any time.

question: Your application needs 6 vCPUs and 40 GB of memory. The predefined machine types either have too little memory or too many vCPUs. What's the most cost-effective option?

options.text: Choose n2-highmem-8 and ignore the unused vCPUs
options.feedback: You'd pay for extra vCPUs you don't need.

options.text: Create a custom machine type with 6 vCPUs and 40 GB of memory
options.feedback: Custom machine types let you choose vCPU and memory amounts, so you pay only for what you need.

options.text: Use two smaller VMs and split memory between them
options.feedback: The application may not support that, and it adds complexity.

options.text: Use an n2-standard-8 Spot VM to offset the extra vCPUs
options.feedback: Spot reduces price but doesn't fix the shape mismatch, and it can be preempted.

takeaway: Custom machine types fit odd CPU-to-memory ratios, and extended memory goes beyond the standard ratio.

question: You've just created a GKE cluster and want to use kubectl from your workstation. Which steps are required? (Choose two.)

options.text: Run gcloud container clusters get-credentials CLUSTER_NAME --location=LOCATION
options.feedback: This writes the cluster endpoint and auth configuration into your kubeconfig.

options.text: Install kubectl and the gke-gcloud-auth-plugin (for example, gcloud components install kubectl gke-gcloud-auth-plugin)
options.feedback: kubectl talks to the API server, and the auth plugin provides Google credentials to kubectl.

options.text: Enable the Cloud Shell API
options.feedback: Cloud Shell isn't required to use kubectl locally.

options.text: SSH into a node and run kubectl there
options.feedback: You don't operate clusters this way, and Autopilot doesn't even allow it.

options.text: Create a service account key and copy it into ~/.kube/config
options.feedback: Keys aren't needed, since gcloud and the auth plugin use your identity.

takeaway: kubectl plus gke-gcloud-auth-plugin plus get-credentials gives you a working kubeconfig.

question: A team wants to run containerized workloads on Kubernetes but doesn't want to manage nodes, node pools, or OS upgrades, and wants to pay for the resources their Pods request. Which GKE mode should they choose?

options.text: GKE Autopilot
options.feedback: Autopilot manages nodes and infrastructure. You're billed mainly for the CPU, memory, and storage your Pods request.

options.text: Cloud Run for Anthos
options.feedback: That isn't the right fit for the requirement. Autopilot is GKE's hands-off mode.

options.text: A single-zone Standard cluster with Spot nodes
options.feedback: This is cheaper but still requires node management.

options.text: GKE Standard with cluster autoscaler
options.feedback: Standard still requires you to manage node pools and pay for whole nodes.

takeaway: Autopilot means Google manages the nodes and you pay per Pod resource request. Standard means you manage node pools and pay per node.

question: Your production GKE cluster must keep its control plane and workloads available during a zone outage. How should you create the cluster?

options.text: Zonal cluster with a large node pool
options.feedback: The control plane and nodes would all be in one zone.

options.text: Two zonal clusters in one zone
options.feedback: A single zone is still a single point of failure.

options.text: Multi-zonal cluster
options.feedback: Nodes spread across zones, but the control plane stays in one zone.

options.text: Regional cluster
options.feedback: Regional clusters run control plane replicas and nodes in several zones for higher availability. Autopilot clusters are always regional.

takeaway: For HA, use a regional GKE cluster, which replicates both the control plane and the nodes.

question: Security requires that GKE nodes have no external IP addresses, while nodes can still pull images from Artifact Registry and reach Google APIs. What should you configure?

options.text: Put the cluster in the default VPC so Google APIs stay reachable
options.feedback: Network choice alone doesn't make nodes private.

options.text: A public cluster with firewall rules denying ingress to nodes
options.feedback: Nodes would still have external IPs, which violates the requirement.

options.text: Use Container-Optimized OS images, which drop external IPs from nodes
options.feedback: The OS choice doesn't control whether nodes get external IPs.

options.text: A private cluster, with Private Google Access enabled on the subnet
options.feedback: Private nodes have no external IPs. Private Google Access lets them reach Google APIs, including Artifact Registry, and Cloud NAT provides other egress.

takeaway: Private nodes plus Private Google Access (plus Cloud NAT for the internet) keeps nodes off the internet but able to pull images.

question: You have a deployment.yaml file that describes your application's Deployment. How do you deploy or update it on your GKE cluster?

options.text: kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
options.feedback: kubectl apply creates or updates resources declaratively from the manifest.

options.text: gcloud run deploy --source=deployment.yaml
options.feedback: That deploys to Cloud Run, not GKE.

options.text: gcloud container clusters create --file=deployment.yaml
options.feedback: That command creates clusters, not workloads.

options.text: kubectl get -f deployment.yaml
options.feedback: get only reads resources.

takeaway: kubectl apply -f is the declarative way to create or update Kubernetes objects.

question: You deployed a web application on GKE and need to expose it to the internet on a public IP through a Google Cloud load balancer. What's the simplest Kubernetes resource to create?

options.text: A Service of type ClusterIP
options.feedback: ClusterIP is internal only.

options.text: A PersistentVolumeClaim
options.feedback: PVCs request storage.

options.text: A ConfigMap with the public IP
options.feedback: ConfigMaps store configuration, not networking.

options.text: A Service of type LoadBalancer
options.feedback: A LoadBalancer Service provisions an external passthrough Network Load Balancer. Ingress or Gateway provision Application Load Balancers.

takeaway: Use LoadBalancer for L4 external exposure, and Ingress or Gateway for L7 HTTP(S) routing, TLS, and path rules.

question: You want a Cloud Run service to be invoked whenever a Compute Engine VM is created anywhere in the project, based on the Admin Activity audit log entry. What should you use?

options.text: A Cloud Storage notification on the project's default bucket
options.feedback: This handles bucket events only.

options.text: A BigQuery scheduled query over the audit log export
options.feedback: This isn't event-driven and is unrelated to VM creation.

options.text: Cloud Scheduler hitting the service every minute to list VMs
options.feedback: Polling is inefficient and delayed.

options.text: An Eventarc audit-log trigger for instance inserts, targeting the service
options.feedback: Eventarc can route events from audit logs, Pub/Sub, Cloud Storage, and more to Cloud Run.

takeaway: Eventarc routes Google Cloud events, including audit-log-based ones, to Cloud Run, GKE, or Workflows.

question: Multiple microservices publish order events. A Cloud Run service must process each event and retry automatically if processing fails. What's a good serverless design?

options.text: Insert events into a Cloud SQL table that the service polls as a queue
options.feedback: A relational database is a poor queue at scale.

options.text: Publish to a Pub/Sub topic with a push subscription to the Cloud Run service
options.feedback: Pub/Sub decouples producers from consumers and retries unacknowledged messages. A dead-letter topic can capture poison messages.

options.text: Call the Cloud Run service directly from every producer and retry in each producer
options.feedback: This couples services tightly and duplicates retry logic.

options.text: Write events to a Cloud Storage bucket and have the service poll it
options.feedback: Polling is slower and you'd have to build retry logic yourself.

takeaway: Pub/Sub push to Cloud Run gives decoupled, retried, at-least-once delivery, and a dead-letter topic handles failures.

question: A research team is training very large transformer models in JAX and wants the best price-performance for large matrix operations at scale. Another team needs CUDA-based libraries for 3D rendering. Which accelerators fit each team?

options.text: TPUs for JAX training, GPUs for CUDA rendering
options.feedback: TPUs are optimized for large tensor and matrix workloads in JAX, TensorFlow, and PyTorch/XLA. CUDA software requires NVIDIA GPUs.

options.text: Local SSDs for both, to speed up I/O
options.feedback: Local SSDs are storage, not accelerators.

options.text: GPUs for both, since they run everything
options.feedback: GPUs work for both, but TPUs are purpose-built for large-scale JAX/TensorFlow training and often give better price-performance there.

options.text: TPUs for both, for the best price
options.feedback: TPUs don't run CUDA workloads.

takeaway: TPUs suit large-scale ML on JAX, TensorFlow, or PyTorch/XLA. GPUs suit CUDA, graphics, and broad framework support.

question: You manage 300 Linux and Windows VMs and need to apply OS patches on a schedule and get compliance reports, without logging into each VM. What should you use?

options.text: Recreate VMs from a new image every night
options.feedback: This is possible for immutable fleets but disruptive, and it gives no compliance reporting.

options.text: A startup script that runs apt upgrade
options.feedback: This only runs at boot, doesn't cover Windows, and gives no reporting.

options.text: Cloud Deploy pipelines that push OS packages
options.feedback: Cloud Deploy releases application versions, not OS patches.

options.text: VM Manager patch deployments across the fleet
options.feedback: VM Manager schedules patch jobs across fleets, supports Linux and Windows, and reports compliance.

takeaway: VM Manager handles OS patching, OS inventory, and OS policies at fleet scale.

question: You need to roll out a new instance template to a managed instance group of 10 VMs without downtime, replacing at most 2 VMs at a time. What should you do?

options.text: Edit each VM's metadata to point at the new template, two at a time
options.feedback: VMs in a MIG should be updated through the template, not individually.

options.text: Start a MIG rolling update to the new template with max-unavailable set to 2
options.feedback: Rolling updates gradually replace instances with the new template and respect max-surge and max-unavailable limits.

options.text: Stop all VMs, change the template, and start them
options.feedback: This causes downtime.

options.text: Delete the MIG and recreate it with the new template
options.feedback: This causes downtime.

takeaway: MIG rolling updates use max-surge and max-unavailable to control the pace. Canary updates can target a subset first.

question: A MIG runs a legacy app where each VM needs to keep its own data disk and hostname through autohealing and updates. What should you configure?

options.text: A stateful MIG that preserves each instance's disk
options.feedback: Stateful MIGs keep instance names, attached disks, and metadata across recreation, autohealing, and updates.

options.text: Local SSDs as the data disks in the template
options.feedback: Local SSD data doesn't survive recreation.

options.text: A regional MIG with autoscaling
options.feedback: Autoscaling would add and remove instances, which conflicts with per-instance state.

options.text: An unmanaged instance group with autohealing
options.feedback: You'd lose autohealing and automated updates.

takeaway: Stateful MIGs preserve disks, names, and metadata for stateful apps while keeping autohealing.

question: Your Cloud Run service must always have at least two instances warm to avoid cold-start latency for user-facing traffic, and at most 50 instances to protect a downstream database. What should you configure?

options.text: Minimum instances 2, maximum instances 50
options.feedback: Min instances keep containers warm, and max instances cap scaling to protect downstream systems.

options.text: CPU always allocated, with 50 max requests
options.feedback: This affects CPU outside requests, not instance counts.

options.text: Concurrency 2, maximum concurrency 50
options.feedback: Concurrency sets requests per instance, not the number of instances.

options.text: A regional MIG behind Cloud Run
options.feedback: Cloud Run doesn't use MIGs that way.

takeaway: Cloud Run min instances reduce cold starts and max instances protect downstream systems.

question: Which two workloads are good fits for Cloud Run? (Choose two.)

options.text: A containerized batch task that runs to completion nightly, using Cloud Run jobs
options.feedback: Cloud Run jobs run containers to completion and can be scheduled with Cloud Scheduler.

options.text: A containerized HTTP API that scales from zero to thousands of requests per second
options.feedback: Request-driven autoscaling with scale to zero is Cloud Run's core use case.

options.text: A stateful database that needs persistent block storage attached to the instance
options.feedback: Cloud Run isn't designed to host databases on persistent block devices. Use a managed database or Compute Engine.

options.text: A workload that needs a custom kernel module and GPUs with full OS access
options.feedback: Kernel-level control needs Compute Engine. Cloud Run abstracts the OS.

options.text: A Windows Server application that needs RDP access
options.feedback: Cloud Run runs Linux containers. It doesn't offer Windows VMs or RDP.

takeaway: Cloud Run services handle requests, and Cloud Run jobs run tasks to completion. Neither fits OS-level control or databases.

question: You need to store regulatory archives that are accessed less than once a year but must be kept for 7 years at the lowest storage cost. Which Cloud Storage class should you use?

options.text: Coldline
options.feedback: Coldline is for data accessed about once a quarter.

options.text: Archive
options.feedback: Archive has the lowest storage price for data accessed less than once a year. It has a 365-day minimum storage duration and higher retrieval costs.

options.text: Nearline
options.feedback: Nearline is for data accessed about once a month.

options.text: Standard
options.feedback: This has the highest storage cost, so it suits frequent access.

takeaway: Minimum storage durations: Standard none, Nearline 30 days, Coldline 90 days, Archive 365 days.

question: Monthly analytics reports are written once and then read about once a month for audits. You want the cheapest class that fits this access pattern. Which should you choose?

options.text: Standard
options.feedback: Standard works but has a higher storage price than needed for monthly access.

options.text: Archive
options.feedback: Retrieval costs and the 365-day minimum make Archive a poor fit for monthly access.

options.text: Nearline
options.feedback: Nearline is designed for data accessed roughly once a month or less, with a 30-day minimum storage duration.

options.text: Coldline
options.feedback: Coldline suits quarterly access, and monthly reads would add retrieval costs.

takeaway: Match the class to access frequency: about monthly is Nearline, about quarterly is Coldline, and yearly or less is Archive.
